structured_output.summary: Ten sources bear on the open hypotheses. Two independent CIFAR results find no gain from stronger orthogonalization: the Polar Express paper's own CIFAR runs, and MUD's airbench table (Muon3 vs Muon5 negligible, MUD1 vs MUD3 too). With E069's 13-seed mean of ~0.7534, this argues the +0.24 pp was a lucky seeds-0-2 draw (H1.2.7/H1.2.9) and lowers the prior for Muon lr 0.20 on the PE base (H1.2.8). Tri Dao's Gram Newton-Schulz post backs the FLOP arithmetic in H2.4.8 (60 vs 84 n^3 at T=3, aspect ratio 9). It also names the bf16 failure modes (spurious negative eigenvalues, eigenvector drift), the 1.05 safety factor and the restart after iteration 2; its measured speedups are only on large transformer matrices, so the end-to-end gain here is ~1% at best. Jordan's airbench and variance papers show seed variance is mostly test-set sampling noise (distribution-wise variance at least 5x smaller), so recipe tweaks cannot shrink the 3-seed gate lottery; only a higher true mean helps (H4). PyTorch docs say deterministic mode disables Inductor's on-device autotuning benchmarking that changes numerics and picks the eager kernel, which points to autotuning as the source of the E077 re-draw (H4.1.7). Hiverge's 1.98 s code gives exact values for intermittent projection (H2.4.3), its NS coefficients, Muon lr/momentum, and a whitening bias trained for only 0.2 epoch; it uses no weight averaging. hlb-CIFAR10's late-started EMA and LAWA's ~1%-of-budget averaging window inform H1.6.1. Untested directions: the airbench 1/9 logit scale (a 10-class value) and per-block Muon lr. Worth checking: whether the airbench96 depth-3 residual was kept in the port. No public CIFAR-100 result beats E069; the fastest public 75% recipe is 8.11 s.

findings.source: arxiv 2505.16932 (Polar Express), CIFAR experiments section (via search summary of the paper)
findings.claim: In the Polar Express paper's own CIFAR experiments, degree-5 Newton-Schulz performs as well as Polar Express despite being much less accurate as a polar approximation. The paper reports no consistent advantage for Polar Express on CIFAR; its gains are on GPT-2-scale language models.
findings.relevance: Direct prior evidence that E069's +0.24 pp on seeds 0-2 was mostly a re-draw, consistent with its 13-seed mean of ~0.7534. Lowers the prior for H1.2.7 and for the paired test in H1.2.9 reaching +0.1 pp. It also weakens the argument for H1.2.8 that Polar Express moved the lr optimum.

findings.claim: Airbench, 8-epoch default: MUD1 93.34% in 2.98 s vs Muon5 94.03% in 3.04 s. 13-epoch setting with momentum 0.7: MUD1 94.07% in 4.75 s vs Muon5 94.44% in 4.82 s. The authors write that stronger orthogonalization does not help on this benchmark: MUD1 to MUD3 adds time without accuracy, and Muon3 to Muon5 gives negligible gains. They also note that 3 NS iterations sometimes caused instabilities in their LM runs.
findings.relevance: A second source saying Muon's accuracy on airbench is flat once orthogonalization is at or above the NS3 default. That fits E017 (NS3 = NS5) and E065 (weaker is a cliff), and argues against a real gain from Polar Express. Weaker decorrelation (MUD1) costs ~0.7 pp at 8 epochs, consistent with E065.

findings.claim: Gram NS iterates on the n x n Gram matrix XX^T. FLOPs: standard NS T(3a+1)n^3, Gram NS with one restart (4T+6a-6)n^3, i.e. 84 vs 60 n^3 at T=3, a=9. In bf16, XX^T develops spurious negative eigenvalues that grow over iterations, and eigenvectors drift. Both are avoided by restarting after iteration 2 (the best bound found for Polar Express coefficients) or by a larger safety factor (default 1.02, recommended 1.05). Polynomials assume ||X0|| <= 1. Fused symmetric GEMMs computing aI + bR + cR^2 can be less stable; the fix is to handle the identity term implicitly in fp32. Measured gains: 40-50% less NS time and up to 2x faster Muon, all on large LM/MoE matrices (aspect ratios 4-8, e.g. 2048x7168).
findings.relevance: Confirms the FLOP arithmetic and stability prescription in H2.4.8 (fp16 or safety factor 1.05, restart after iteration 2). No evidence on small batched matrices like 128x1152; the cuSOLVER-free bmm path there may be latency-bound. With the whole Muon step at ~6% of the run, the end-to-end ceiling is ~1-1.5%.

findings.claim: Exact settings: NS coefficients (3.4576, -4.7391, 2.0843). Pre-NS update magnitude decays linearly from 0.5012 to 0.0786. Muon(lr=0.205, momentum=0.655, nesterov=True, weight_decay=wd). The weight-norm projection runs every norm_freq steps, with norm_freq = 2 + int(15*progress). No lookahead or EMA at all. Batch size 1536, 7.65 epochs, label smoothing 0.09. Whitening bias trained only for ceil(0.2*steps_per_epoch) steps, with its own linear lr decay. Separate lrs: biases 0.0573, head 0.5415. Linear warmdown to 0. Selective TTA on the 25% least-confident samples (not allowed under these rules).
findings.relevance: Gives exact parameters for H2.4.3 (intermittent projection, ~2-17 step interval). Hiverge pairs it with Muon weight decay, which the tip lacks, so dropping projection steps without wd may let weight norms drift. Shows the whitening bias can be trained for only 0.2 epoch (tip: 1 epoch, E034/E060 flat), a small extra time cut. Confirms Hiverge's magnitude schedule is not RMS-matched (H1.9).

findings.source: arxiv 2404.00498 (airbench paper); arxiv 2304.01910 (Jordan, variance in NN training)
findings.claim: Across 10,000 airbench94 runs, every case has at least 5x less distribution-wise variance than test-set variance. Seed-to-seed spread in test accuracy is mostly finite-sample test-set noise, from approximately independent per-example errors (a consequence of class calibration), not training instability. Lookahead (decay 0.95^5 x (t/T)^3, every 5 steps) cut epochs to 94% from 18 to 12 on CIFAR-10.
findings.relevance: No recipe change can meaningfully reduce the 3-seed gate's variance. The only way through the gate is a true-mean gain of ~+0.2 pp, or bundling time cuts with such a gain. Supports H4/H4.4 and the 13-seed scoring practice. Also suggests the 40-seed official mean is very stable (H4.3).

findings.source: PyTorch docs: torch.use_deterministic_algorithms / Inductor deterministic mode
findings.claim: With deterministic algorithms enabled, Inductor's deterministic mode also turns on: it avoids on-device benchmarking that affects numerics. Without it, Inductor autotunes matmul/conv templates and adopts a template kernel if it is faster than eager, so kernel choice, and therefore rounding, can differ between processes.
findings.relevance: Documents the mechanism behind E077's process-level re-draw (H4.1.7). The PyTorch docs above describe current behaviour, so check the flag exists in 2.4 before relying on it. Deterministic or pinned-cache kernel selection would make offline seed checks match the harness, but it does not change the recipe's expected accuracy and should not be used to select on seeds 0-2. It would cost the ~1% max-autotune gain (H2.5.1).

findings.claim: hlb-CIFAR10's EMA (from which airbench's lookahead derives) starts only for the last 10 of 12.1 epochs, initialized from the current weights rather than the initial ones. It uses decay_base 0.95, decay_pow 3 (decay x (t/T)^3) and updates every 5 steps. The comments describe it as like Lookahead but with a much more aggressive-at-the-end schedule.
findings.relevance: Prior art for the H1.6.1 candidates. An EMA layered on lookahead, started late from the current weights with a cubic ramp, has a precedent but no published head-to-head numbers. E028 (0.95^5 to 0.97^5) suggests the horizon is flat, so ramp shape or sync interval are the remaining knobs. Expected gain is small.

findings.source: arxiv 2306.03241 / 2209.14981 (LAWA); arxiv 2502.06761 (When, Where and Why to Average Weights)
findings.claim: LAWA (averaging the latest checkpoints) beats Lookahead on CIFAR-100 ResNet-34 and reaches high accuracy much earlier. An averaging window of about 1% of the training budget is reported as optimal in that study. On AlgoPerf, averaging speeds up training across workloads and interacts with lr annealing.
findings.relevance: Weak, long-horizon evidence for H1.6.1: averaging-window tuning can matter, but the airbench lookahead is already a strong, aggressive-at-the-end averager. Low expected gain at 6.75 epochs.

findings.claim: airbench96's depth-3 ConvGroup has a residual connection (x = conv3(...); x = x + x0). The logits are multiplied by a fixed scaling_factor of 1/9. BatchNorm uses eps=1e-12 with weight disabled and bias only, and runs in float32 at inference. Hyperparameters: lr 9.0 per 1024, bias_scaler 64, Nesterov momentum 0.85, decoupled wd 0.012, label smoothing 0.2.
findings.relevance: Two untested knobs. (1) The 1/9 logit scale was tuned for 10 classes. With 100 classes, logit scale (temperature) interacts with the head lr (x2 helped, x3 = x2) and with the gradient sent back to the features. A 1-line probe would vary it. (2) Check whether the port kept the depth-3 residual; if dropped, re-adding it is a candidate accuracy gain at ~0 cost.

findings.source: arxiv 2609.09676 (Muon-C: Operator-Aligned Muon for Convolutional Kernels)
findings.claim: Muon-C orthogonalizes one C_out x C_in matrix per spatial DFT frequency (complex Fourier modes, not a real DCT), with matched-RMS scaling 0.2/RMS(O). It costs 15.5% more per step than flattened Muon. It wins on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 flow-matching (FID 3.42 vs 3.54 tuned), but no airbench or short classification results are reported.
findings.relevance: E030 tested a real-DCT variant, not Muon-C itself, but the evidence for Muon-C is from long generative training only, and the per-frequency equalization mechanism E030 identified still applies. Keeps the kernel-split branch closed for this regime.
